title: DLSS 5 turns 1991's Sonic the Hedgehog into a weird neural network experiment.
key_facts: Enthusiasts ran the original 1991 Sega Mega Drive Sonic the Hedgehog through Nvidia's DLSS 5 neural rendering, using RenoDX and ReShade tools in the frame output, with Multipass x4 processing.
DLSS 5, introduced by Nvidia in 2026, uses AI to generate pixels, lighting and materials in real time.
Four profiles were tried on the Green Hill Zone level: Natural, Default, Cinematic and Denoise.
The Default profile gave the pixelated hedgehog pronounced cheekbones and a pseudo-realistic skull shape; Cinematic added dramatic lighting.
The aggressive Denoise profile erased the golden rings, palm foliage and nearly all ground detail.
The site says Sonic's speed stops the AI from producing a consistent image of the character, while jump and acceleration physics stay unchanged.
quote_evidence: The original Sonic the Hedgehog platformer, released in 1991 for the Sega Mega Drive, was benchmarked using DLSS 5.0 neural network rendering technology.
The Default profile attempts to reconstruct the protagonist's facial anatomy, giving the pixelated hedgehog pronounced cheekbones and a pseudo-realistic skull shape.
The testing demonstrates both the capabilities of the neural network pipeline and its obvious technical limitations when directly processing classic pixel graphics without specialized model training.
why_it_matters_hint: A playful stress test shows where AI graphics rendering breaks down on fast 2D pixel art.
notes: The enthusiasts are not named; a single site reports it, in somewhat machine-translated English.
